corpus.source: CISI digitisation (Carlson, MIT licence), Mohenjo-daro M-1–M-199

replay.prompt: If there's only 400–600 symbols, how many finite combinations are there? Let's try it.
replay.answer: With 709 signs (Wells/Fuls list) the possible strings grow as 709ⁿ: about 5.0×10⁵ pairs, 3.6×10⁸ triples and 9.0×10¹⁹ seven-sign strings. Brute force over that space is not a method. What can be counted is what actually occurs. In the 179 seals in hand, these are the distinct sequences of each length:

rays.purpose: the seals themselves, in reading order

rays.name: Present-day Indus Valley
rays.purpose: modern languages of the region — no data loaded

rays.name: Lexicon
rays.purpose: signs on the core surface, 2–7-sign strings on the inner walls

rays.name: Artifact Repository
rays.purpose: CISI files nested inside the Lexicon core

rays.name: Comparative
rays.purpose: Zipf slope and entropy against shuffled text

rays.name: Reverse-engineering IETF
rays.purpose: present day → past; needs language data not in hand

rays.name: Dream Engine
rays.purpose: samples new seals from the learned model

eve.note: With every r_i equal, rays spread evenly over the sphere nearly cancel, so |S| is small. S only grows in a direction when the NVEs pointing that way carry more evidence. S is therefore a weighted resultant: it says which rays dominate, not how much was decoded.
eve.k_ge_1: Σ k^n diverges for |k| ≥ 1 — S is infinite unless the series is cut off (pass n_terms).
